text:
Her Majesty the Queen v. N. S. et al.; Ontario Human

Rights Commission, Intervenor

[Indexed as: R. v. S. (N.)]

95 O.R. (3d) 735

Ontario Superior Court of Justice,

Marrocco J.

April 30, 2009

Criminal law -- Preliminary inquiry -- Complainant wishing to testify at preliminary inquiry while wearing veil -- Preliminary hearing judge questioning complainant in order to assess the strength of her religious objection to removing her veil without permitting her to consult counsel -- Preliminary hearing judge ruling that complainant being ordered to remove veil before testifying -- Complainant seeking order quashing direction to remove veil and order that she be permitted to testify with veil -- Complainant prejudiced by being prevented from consulting counsel before being questioned and decision ordering that veil be removed before she testifies at preliminary hearing quashed -- Preliminary hearing judge also erring by purporting to balance Charter values as not court of competent jurisdiction -- Superior Court judge holding that preliminary hearing judge has jurisdiction to conduct hearing within preliminary hearing to determine whether witness should be permitted to testify while wearing a veil -- During the hearing within hearing witness should be permitted to wear veil and evidence should be taken on oath -- Preliminary hearing judge having power to order that veil be removed based on evidence at hearing within hearing -- If witness refuses to remove veil when ordered judge may decline to receive her evidence -- Superior Court judge declining to make order sought by complainant that she be permitted to wear veil while testifying at preliminary hearing and remitting issue back to lower court while providing directions as to how to proceed when issue of witness wearing veil arises at preliminary inquiry including that hearing regarding veil should be videotaped to permit meaningful judicial review.
The two accused were charged with historical sexual offences against the applicant. At the time of the preliminary inquiry, the applicant was a 32-year-old married woman who customarily wore a veil (niqab) in public. The accused sought an order requiring the applicant to testify without a veil. The preliminary inquiry judge questioned the unrepresented applicant informally and concluded that her religious belief was not that strong, that it was open to exceptions and [page736] that wearing the veil was a matter of comfort. He ordered her to remove her veil while testifying. In reaching that conclusion, he indicated that he was aware that his decision was informed by
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
considerations, that he started with the proposition that the accused had a fundamental right to make full answer and defence and to face their accuser, and that he had to balance the applicant's freedom of religion against that right. The applicant brought an application to quash that order and for an order permitting her to wear her veil when testifying at the preliminary inquiry.
Held, the application should be granted in part.
The preliminary inquiry judge exceeded his jurisdiction by balancing
Charter
values, which he could not do as he was not a court of competent jurisdiction. Moreover, his ruling that the applicant answer questions about her reasons for wearing a veil without the benefit of counsel was clearly prejudicial to the applicant, as was his decision, which was based in part on the applicant's response to those questions. The decision was quashed.
In determining whether the applicant should be required to testify without a veil, the preliminary inquiry judge should conduct a hearing to resolve two issues. First, the court must determine the applicant's reasons for believing that she must wear her veil. The applicant should be a witness and should be permitted at that point to testify wearing her veil. The applicant's evidence should be received on oath or affirmation. Counsel for the accused and the Crown should be permitted to question the applicant. The onus is on the applicant to demonstrate that her fundamental freedom of religion has been triggered. If the preliminary inquiry judge is not satisfied that the applicant is wearing a veil for a religious or other valid reason, he has the authority pursuant to
s. 537(1)
of the
Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46
to order her to remove it. If the preliminary inquiry judge decides that the applicant is wearing her veil for a religious or other valid reason, then he must determine the second issue: whether he can comply with s. 540(1) of the Code if the applicant is veiled when she testifies. Specifically, he must decide whether the applicant can be cross-examined as that term is understood in the context of s. 540(1). The preliminary inquiry judge should conduct a second hearing within the preliminary inquiry to determine that question. The applicant should be called and examined in chief by the Crown, and defence counsel should attempt to cross- examine. The applicant should testify concerning the substance of the charges while veiled. If the preliminary inquiry judge decides that cross-examination has taken place, then the evidence offered by the applicant will be admitted at the preliminary inquiry subject to arguments about relevance. If he is of the view that cross-examination has not taken place, the evidence will not be admitted at the preliminary inquiry. In order to permit meaningful judicial review, the applicant's testimony on this second hearing within the preliminary inquiry should be videotaped.
While a Superior Court judge granting prerogative relief has jurisdiction to grant an additional remedy pursuant to
s. 24(1)
of the
Charter
, this would not be an appropriate case in which to make an order permitting the applicant to testify at the preliminary inquiry while veiled in the absence of an appropriate record. That record should properly be created as part of the preliminary hearing rather than on this motion.
APPLICATION to quash a decision of a preliminary inquiry judge requiring the applicant to testify without a veil and for an order permitting the applicant to testify at the preliminary inquiry while veiled.

Laurie Gonet, for respondent Her Majesty the Queen.
David Butt, for applicant.
J. Pinkofsky, for respondent M----D. S.
M----L. S. not present.
Prabhu Rajan, for intervenor. [page738]

[
1
] MARROCCO J.: -- The applicant requests two orders. The
first quashes an order of Judge Weisman made October 16, 2008,
during the course of a preliminary inquiry, requiring the
applicant to remove her veil during her testimony. The second
requests an order permitting the applicant to wear her veil
when testifying at the preliminary inquiry in this matter. The
first request is granted. The second is refused.
The History of the Preliminary Inquiry Proceedings

[
2
] There were two informations before His Honour Judge
Weisman. His Honour was, as a practical matter, conducting one
preliminary inquiry in respect of both informations.

[
3
] M----D. S. was charged alone on one information with
indecent assault, gross indecency and sexual assault. The
offences are alleged to have occurred at different times
between September 1, 1982 and June 30, 1987. The applicant is
the complainant on all charges.

[
4
] M----D. S. was arrested on June 20, 2007. He was released
on bail on June 22, 2007. Disclosure was completed on October
9, 2007. His preliminary inquiry was set for September 10 and
11, 2008. On September 10, 2008, MD. S. formally elected to be
tried by a court composed of a judge and jury.

[
5
] M----L. S. was charged on a separate information with
indecent assault, gross indecency, sexual assault and with
having sexual intercourse with the applicant at a time when she
was under 14 years of age. These offences are alleged to have
occurred at different times between September 1, 1982 and June
30, 1987. The applicant is the complainant on all charges.

[
6
] M----L. S. was arrested on June 20, 2007. He was released
on bail June 22, 2007. Disclosure was provided on December 3,
2007. His preliminary inquiry was set for September 10 and 11,
2008. On September 10, 2008, he formally elected to be tried by
a court composed of a judge and jury.

[
7
] At the request of the defence, Judge Weisman made an
order banning publication of the evidence heard at the
preliminary inquiry. At the request of the Crown, Judge Weisman
made an order banning the publication of any information which
would identify the applicant.
The History of the Veil Motion at the Preliminary Inquiry

[
8
] On September 10, 2008, an application was brought by the
defendants which is found at tab 3 of the Application Record.
The application requested an order requiring the applicant to
testify without a veil. The application was filed on September
10, 2008 at the commencement of the preliminary inquiry.
[page739]

[
9
] The Crown at the preliminary inquiry, not the Crown
appearing on this application, advised the preliminary inquiry
judge, without objection, that she had asked counsel for the
defendant, M----D. S., on the preceding Thursday (September 4)
whether he intended to apply for such an order and that counsel
refused to tell her what he was going to do. Counsel for the
defendant M----D. S. on this application, who was not counsel
at the preliminary inquiry, refused to accept the truthfulness
of this representation.

[
10
] The motion was argued intermittently on September 10 and
11, 2008. In addition, witnesses other than the applicant were
called to testify. Only one of these witnesses was required by
the Crown for purposes of the preliminary inquiry. The other
witnesses were called so that the defendants might further
discover the Crown's case.

[
11
] On September 10 counsel for the defendants advised that
their clients were prepared to admit that the applicant's
reason for wishing to testify while veiled was due to a
religious belief. On September 10, 2008, in response to the
defendants' motion, a police officer asked the applicant if she
would testify without a veil. The applicant refused.

[
12
] On September 11, 2008, the Crown disclosed this
conversation to counsel for the defendants who then advised
that they would no longer admit the sincerity of the
applicant's belief. Counsel insisted upon cross-examining the
applicant on this issue. This was an odd turn of events because
one of the defendants is the applicant's uncle and both
defendants attend the same mosque as the applicant's family.
They presumably knew she was sincere about her religious belief
when they agreed to that fact on the previous day.

[
13
] In response to the defendants' change in position, the
Crown asked the court to give the applicant an opportunity to
obtain legal advice. The preliminary inquiry judge decided to
immediately question the applicant. He decided that he would
not permit the Crown or defence to ask her any questions.

[
14
] His Honour then asked the applicant questions in open
court which she answered. She was veiled while this occurred.
The applicant was not asked to take an oath or otherwise bind
her conscience. The motion concerning the removal of the veil
was adjourned to October 16, 2008 for further argument. The
preliminary inquiry was adjourned to March 9, 2009.

[
15
] On October 16, 2008, the preliminary inquiry judge gave
the ruling which is the subject of this motion and which is
found at tab 6 of the Application Record. If there was further
argument that day, the transcript was not filed. [page740]
The Position of the Defendants before the Preliminary Inquiry
Judge

[
16
] Neither of the defendants filed affidavits in support of
their application.

[
17
] Counsel for M----D. S. argued that he should be able to
"witness the demeanour of the witness". He submitted that he
was asking for an evidentiary ruling based on common-law
principles which the preliminary inquiry judge had jurisdiction
to make.

[
18
] Specifically, he made the following submission: "seeing
the demeanour of the witness is a matter of critical importance
not only at the trial but also at the preliminary inquiry. My
cross-examination is determined by my assessment of the
demeanour of the witness. I may be pursuing a certain line of
questioning for the witness. Having an opportunity to see their
demeanour, I might conclude I believe the witness is being
sincere on this point, am I really going to get anywhere with
this line of questioning, no, I do not think I am, move on to
somewhere else. On the other hand upon observing a witness's
demeanour, I might conclude, easily, that the witness is
prevaricating, the witness is not being forthright and I may
want to explore that area further."

[
19
] Counsel also submitted it was a matter of making full
answer and defence. Specifically, he said "so it is a question
of making full answer and defence. It is a question of being
prepared for the nature of the witness you will meet at trial .
. . ".

[
20
] Counsel for M----L. S. adopted those submissions. In
addition on the question of jurisdiction, he said that their
motion would encompass [the] right to make full answer and
defence, which he said was part of his client's rights under
the rules of natural justice. He argued that the ability to
question or to assess or to view the demeanour of a witness
assisted in terms of the nature of the defence and directed the
cross-examination.

[
21
] The preliminary inquiry judge immediately ruled that he
had jurisdiction to order the removal of the veil.
Interestingly, His Honour ruled as well that there was no
absolute right even at trial to observe the demeanour of the
witness and refused the request to order the removal of the
veil.

[
22
] Counsel for the defendants then objected to the ruling
on the basis that they had not completed their submissions. The
preliminary inquiry judge agreed to reconsider after hearing
the balance of their submissions. Counsel for the defendants
were directed to return the next day, September 11, 2008, for
that purpose. [page741]

[
23
] The next day, counsel took the position as I stated
earlier, that they were no longer willing to admit that the
applicant was motivated by a religious belief and the applicant
was questioned without being sworn by the preliminary inquiry
judge. No further argument was made on the substance of the
motion. If further argument occurred, it occurred on October
16, 2008.
The Position of the Crown before the Preliminary Inquiry Judge

[
24
] The Crown took the position that the applicant ought to
be permitted to wear "this article of religious dress". The
Crown argued that the issue was fundamentally a
Canadian
Charter of Rights and Freedoms
issue which should be
adjudicated at trial.

[
25
] The Crown's view was that, given the purpose of the
preliminary inquiry, matters relating to demeanour and
credibility overall were issues for trial. The Crown argued
that cross-examination was not being avoided. The applicant
would answer questions posed by defence counsel, her words
would be heard by everyone as would her tone of voice. Her body
language would be visible. The Crown submitted that the
specific aspects of demeanour of concern to the defence came
from seeing the lower part of the applicant's face.
The Position of the Applicant before the Preliminary Inquiry
Judge

[
26
] When the preliminary inquiry judge indicated that he
wished to hear from the applicant, the Crown indicated that she
was seeking, with the assistance of the Victim Witness
Assistance Program, outside counsel for her and asked His
Honour to wait until counsel had been retained before asking
her any questions. Counsel for M----D. S. agreed that the
applicant be questioned without waiting for her to obtain
counsel but submitted she should be under oath.

[
27
] His Honour questioned the applicant immediately. The
applicant was veiled and not sworn or affirmed. Prior to the
questioning, the preliminary inquiry judge stated that, if the
applicant insisted wearing a veil was a religious issue, she
would be given the opportunity to obtain legal advice.

[
28
] The applicant who was not at the courthouse was
contacted by the police and immediately attended. The
preliminary inquiry judge told the applicant that he wanted to
hear from her on an informal basis concerning why she objected
to removing her veil while testifying. He told her that no one
else would ask her any questions but himself. He told her that
he wanted to know how strong her objection was.

[
29
] The applicant said her objection was very strong. She
said "it is a respect issue, one of modesty and one of -- in
Islam we [page742] call honour. The other thing is . . . the
accuseds in the case are from the same community, they all go
to the same place of worship as my husband as well and I have
had this veil on for about five years now and it is -- my face
does not make any special, you know, like I know that -- you
know, there's body language, there's eye contact. I mean, I can
look directly at the defence counsel, that is not a problem."
[and] " . . . it is a part of me and showing my face to
-- and it is also about -- the religious reason is not to show
your face to men that you are able to marry. It is to conceal
the beauty of a woman and, you know, we are in a courtroom full
of men and one of the accused is not a direct family member.
The other accused is a direct family member and I, you know, I
would feel a lot more comfortable if I didn't have to, you
know, reveal my face. You know, just considering the nature of
the case and the nature of the allegations and I think, you
know, my face is not going to show any signs of -- it is not
going to help, it really won't." Finally, the applicant said
she wore a veil in public but did not wear a veil in the
presence of family members.
Judge Weisman's Reasons and Decision

[
30
] The preliminary inquiry judge gave his decision as I
indicated earlier, on October 16, 2008. On this date, counsel
for the applicant appeared on her behalf.

[
31
] His Honour repeated the conclusion he reached earlier,
namely, that he was deciding an evidentiary issue and therefore
a matter within his jurisdiction.

[
32
] His Honour indicated that he was aware that his decision
was informed by
Charter
considerations. He indicated that he
started with the proposition that the accused had a fundamental
right to make full answer and defence and to face their
accuser. The court advised that it was aware of cases from the
Ontario Court of Appeal diminishing the importance of
demeanour. His Honour stated that he had to balance N.S.'s
strong religious feeling that it was sinful to bare her
features.

[
33
] The court indicated that it was taking into account the
strength of the applicant's religious belief. His Honour stated
that he was taking into consideration how important her
constitutional right to freedom of religion was to her. His
Honour pointed out that he now knew that the applicant had a
driver's licence with her unveiled face on it. The court
indicated that the admitted facts were that the photograph was
taken by a female photographer in an open office with a screen
between the applicant and male onlookers. The preliminary
inquiry judge observed that the applicant's reasoning, namely,
that these procedures [page743] satisfied her, was specious
because she would have to produce her driver's licence to
police and border guards. The court found that the applicant's
decision to pose for the photograph was not consistent with the
strength of her belief about showing her face.

[
34
] Finally, His Honour stated that, although the decision
was difficult, the applicant would have to remove her veil. Her
religious belief was not that strong. It was open to exceptions
and wearing the veil was a matter of comfort.

[
35
] After this ruling, the preliminary inquiry was
adjourned, the applicant brought this application and the
Ontario Human Rights Commission applied for intervenor status.
The History of this Proceeding

[
36
] On November 14, 2008, the applicant moved for
extraordinary remedies in the nature of certiorari and mandamus
as well as a remedy under
s. 24(1)
of the
Charter of Rights
.

[
37
] This application was returnable December 8, 2008. On
that date, the applicant adjourned this matter to December 17,
2008. The endorsement on the application provided that it was
to be spoken to at that time. On December 17, 2008, the motion
was adjourned to January 26, 2009 to be argued. It was
estimated that the motion would take two hours. On January 26,
2009, the application was not argued; it was adjourned to March
2, 2009 for argument. It was estimated that the application
would take three hours.

[
38
] On March 2, 2009, the application had not been perfected
and so a timetable was set. It was decided that there was some
urgency to the matter because M----D. S.'s counsel complained
that his client's
Charter
right to a trial within a reasonable
time was infringed by the time taken to conclude this motion.
The other defendant M----L. S., although served with notice of
this application, took no part in these proceedings.

[
39
] The timetable required the applicant to file materials
on March 3, 2009. The Ontario Human Rights Commission was to
file materials on March 4, 2009. The Crown was to file on March
5, 2009. The defendant, M----D. S., was to file on March 6,
2009. All parties agreed that the matter would be argued on
March 13, 2009.

[
40
] With the exception of counsel for M----D. S., the other
parties complied with the timetable. Due to the fact that
counsel for M----D. S. failed to comply, a new timetable was
set. The defendant was to file materials on March 23, 2009 and
the motion was to be argued March 25 and 27, 2009. Counsel for
M----D. S. failed to file materials on March 23, 2009 and
another timetable [page744] was set. It was ordered that the
motion would be argued on March 27, 2009 and April 3, 2009. It
was further ordered that oral argument would conclude by 1:00
p.m. on April 3, 2009. The applicant, the Crown and the Ontario
Human Rights Commission would have the opportunity to file a
written reply to any oral argument advanced by M----D. S.

[
41
] Oral argument concluded on April 3, 2009 at 1:00 p.m.,
however counsel for the defendant M----D. S. had not completed
his oral submissions and was given until April 14, 2009 to
complete his submissions in writing. Counsel for the applicant,
the Crown and the Ontario Human Rights Commission were given
until April 21, 2009 to file submissions replying to any
matters raised by counsel for M----D. S. in oral or written
argument. Counsel for M----D. S. failed to file any written
submissions. The applicant and the Crown filed written reply
within the time agreed upon.
The Position of the Applicant on this Application

[
42
] Counsel for the applicant took no position on the
application to intervene.

[
43
] The applicant submitted that she was denied procedural
fairness. The applicant submitted her position was prejudiced
by this procedural error because, contrary to her religious
belief that it was necessary for her to cover her face with the
exception of her eyes, she was now required to reveal her face.

[
44
] Counsel submitted that this procedural error resulted in
a loss of jurisdiction.

[
45
] Counsel also submitted that the preliminary inquiry
judge drifted from considering the manner in which the
applicant was going to testify to granting
Charter
relief to
the defendants, which he had no jurisdiction to do.

[
46
] Counsel submitted that the preliminary inquiry judge
should have permitted the applicant to testify wearing a veil
and should have permitted counsel for the defendants to lay a
foundation for a
Charter
challenge at trial to her right to do
that.

[
47
] It was submitted that I should remit the matter to the
preliminary inquiry judge with the instruction that he do that.

[
48
] Counsel for the applicant submitted on the merits of the

Charter
issue that the applicant's veil negligibly affected her
demeanour because there were a host of demeanour clues still
available and that demeanour was a discredited tool for
determining whether a witness was telling the truth. [page745]
The Position of the Intervenor Ontario Human Rights Commission

[
49
] The intervenor (the Human Rights Commission) made no
submissions on the question of jurisdiction conceding that it
had no particular expertise in this area.

[
50
] The Human Rights Commission pointed out that no right or
freedom is absolute.

[
51
] The Human Rights Commission submitted that there was an
onus on the applicant to demonstrate that her fundamental
freedom of religion had been triggered.

[
52
] The Human Rights Commission maintained that the
fundamental freedom of conscience and religion and the legal
right to make full answer and defence included in
s. 7
of the

Charter
were competing Charter rights. Conflicts between
competing rights must be reconciled. In the Human Rights
Commission's view, a
s. 1
Charter analysis was required unless
the interference with one of the competing rights was minimal.
It was also pointed out that
s. 1
required that any
accommodation minimally interfere with the rights or freedoms
affected.

[
53
] Finally, it suggested a
s. 1
analysis would be difficult
due to the meagre record before this court.
The Position of the Respondent Crown

[
54
] The Crown took the view that that the application to
intervene should be refused. The Crown put this forward as an
issue to be decided on jurisdictional grounds and that the
Human Rights Commission had no expertise that would be helpful.

[
55
] It was the Crown's position that the preliminary inquiry
judge described and then dealt with the
Charter
issues raised
in this application and thereby exceeded his jurisdiction. The
Crown submitted that in substance the preliminary inquiry judge
weighed the applicant's religious freedom against the accuseds'
right to make full answer and defence. It was suggested that I
disregard the preliminary inquiry judge's ruling that he was
dealing with the manner in which the applicant would testify.

[
56
] The Crown submitted that it was premature for me to
decide whether a witness can testify at a criminal trial

Analysis

The application to intervene

[
70
] The application to intervene is allowed. The Human
Rights Commission has a real, substantial and identifiable
interest in this matter.
Section 29
of the
Human Rights Code,
R.S.O. 1990, c. H.19
sets out the Human Rights Commission's
mandate, which is to "promote and advance respect for human
rights in Ontario, to protect human rights in Ontario and,
recognizing that it is in the public interest to do so and that
is the commission's duty to protect the public interest to
identify and promote the elimination of discriminatory
practices . . .".

[
71
] Secondly, these issues will arise again. In that regard,
counsel for the defendant took the position that a veiled
person should not be permitted to sit on a jury.

[
72
] Accordingly, I accept that the participation of veiled
persons in the criminal justice system is alive in this
proceeding and that a matter of public policy is engaged which
is broader than the interest of the parties.

[
73
] The Human Rights Commission clearly has expertise in
this area and therefore is able to help the court appreciate
fully the human rights implications of any decision. I note
that the Human Rights Commission has been permitted to
intervene in religious rights cases in the past.

[
74
] The Human Rights Commission made one submission in
support of its application to intervene which I reject. It
suggested [page748] that permission to intervene can be granted
to prevent an injustice to one party to a proceeding. The
applicant is well-represented and needs no such assistance.
Secondly, the Human Rights Commission's utility is tied to its
commitment to the public interest as opposed to the interest of
a party.

[
75
] Accordingly, the application to intervene is granted.
The Human Rights Commission's oral and written submissions on
the merits of the application are before the court.

Section 37
of the
Canada Evidence Act

[
76
]
Section 37
of the
Canada Evidence Act
deals with
specified public interests. This is an application concerning a
personal right. Section 37 has no application.

The preliminary inquiry judge's decision

[
77
] His Honour was conducting a preliminary inquiry. He was
not conducting trial. He had no jurisdiction to acquit or
convict. He could not impose a penalty nor could he give a
remedy. He was not a court of competent jurisdiction and
therefore had no jurisdiction to hear and determine whether a

Charter
right had been infringed: see R. v. Mills,
1986 CanLII 17 (SCC)
, [1986] 1
S.C.R. 863, [1986] S.C.J. No. 39, at para.
265
.

[
78
] The record before me does not disclose what the
applicant looked like when she appeared before the preliminary
inquiry judge. There is no picture nor is there a description
except the assertion by the defence counsel that she wears a
veil which covers her face. In future, when these matters
arise, in order to permit meaningful judicial review, the
preliminary inquiry judge should insist that the contentious
portion of the proceedings involving the veiled witness be
videotaped. Visual aids are important because the absence of
visual clues is the cause for complaint.

[
79
] The context in which the applicant was appearing is
important. In the future when these matters arise, the
preliminary inquiry judge should ensure that the factual
allegation is part of the record. On this application, the
Crown, at the invitation of the court, filed a synopsis of the
allegations.

[
80
] The applicant, who is now a 32-year-old adult married
woman, complains of sexual abuse from the time she was six
years old. She recounted to police a childhood plagued with
sexual assaults. This matter was first investigated by the
police in 1992 because the applicant complained to a teacher.
The applicant's father insisted that no charges be laid and the
police reluctantly agreed. In May 2007, the applicant, who was
at that time the mother of three and expecting a fourth, asked
the police to [page749] re-open the matter, indicating she
could not forget the sexual abuse she suffered and the matter
was improperly handled by her father.

[
81
] When objection was taken to the applicant's appearance,
the preliminary inquiry judge had to determine whether he was
going to use his authority under
s. 537(1)
of the
Criminal Code

to regulate the course of the inquiry to require the applicant
to remove her veil when testifying. In making this decision,
His Honour was required to consider
s. 540(1)
of the Criminal
Code, which mandated him to allow the accused or counsel for
the accused to cross-examine prosecution witnesses.

[
82
] In an effort to resolve the objection, the preliminary
inquiry judge took over the proceedings. He called the
applicant himself, declined to hear her evidence under oath and
questioned her exclusively. He advised the applicant that he
was going to question her "just on a very informal basis" and
then treated her responses as central to his decision.

[
83
] His Honour started out with the premise that he was
dealing with the manner in which the applicant gave evidence;
however, as his reasoning progressed, he balanced
Charter

values which he cannot do because he is not a court of
competent jurisdiction.

[
84
] His Honour exceeded his jurisdiction. Certiorari lies to
cure an excess of jurisdiction: see R. v. Forsythe,
1980 CanLII 15 (SCC)
, [1980] 2
S.C.R. 268, [1980] S.C.J. No. 66.

[
85
] His Honour's ruling that the applicant answer questions
about her reasons for wearing a veil without the benefit of
counsel, other than the Crown Attorney who was conflicted on
the matter, was clearly prejudicial to the applicant. The same
can be said for the decision under review which was based in
part on the applicant's responses to the same questions.

[
86
] Accordingly, his decision is quashed.
Directions

[
87
] I propose now, pursuant to this court's supervisory
jurisdiction, to provide directions.

[
88
] To put the matter shortly, the preliminary inquiry judge
should conduct a hearing, within the preliminary inquiry, to
resolve the issues created by the defendants' application and
the applicant's objection to removing her veil. His Honour has
jurisdiction pursuant to
s. 537(1)
to order the veil removed.
If the applicant refuses to comply with the order, the court,
among other things, has the option of refusing to admit her
evidence on the preliminary inquiry itself. A preliminary
inquiry judge has [page750] jurisdiction to conduct a hearing
within the preliminary inquiry: see R. v. Pickett,
1975 CanLII 1428 (ON CA)
, [1975] O.J.
No. 675, 28 C.C.C. (2d) 297 (C.A.).

[
89
] Two issues must be resolved. Firstly, the court must
determine the applicant's reasons for believing that she must
wear her veil. The applicant should be a witness and should be
permitted at this point to testify wearing her veil. To require
its removal at this stage would prejudge the matter. The
applicant's evidence should be received on oath or affirmation.
Counsel for the defendants and the Crown should be permitted to
question the applicant. His Honour should call the applicant as
a witness. All of the applicant's reasons, religious or
otherwise, are relevant and should be explored.

[
90
] On this application, the applicant's reason for wearing
a veil has been described as religious and so I propose to
comment on the matter.
Religious Belief

[
91
] The onus is on the applicant to demonstrate that her
fundamental freedom of religion has been triggered.

[
92
] The Supreme Court of Canada discussed what is meant by a
religious belief in the case of Syndicat Northcrest v. Amselem,

2004 SCC 47 (CanLII)
, [2004] 2 S.C.R. 551, [2004] S.C.J. No. 46. In that case the
appellants, all Orthodox Jews, were divided co-owners of
residential units in two luxury buildings in Montreal. They
wanted to build a biblically mandated hut on their balconies.
The huts would remain in place for nine days each year and then
be removed. The other owners objected, claiming that the huts
interfered with their right to enjoy their property. In
resolving the matter, the court was required to consider the
right of a minority to pursue its religious beliefs and the
extent to which that right was protected by the
Quebec Charter
of human rights and freedoms, R.S.Q., c. C-12
.

[
93
] At para. 56 of the judgment, the majority said that an
individual advancing an issue premised upon a freedom of
religion must show (1) that she has a practice or belief,
having a nexus with religion, which calls for particular
conduct; and (2) that she is sincere in her practice or belief.

[
94
] In addition, the Supreme Court of Canada has said that
the essence of freedom of religion is the right to entertain
religious beliefs chosen freely in the absence of coercion or
restraint: see R. v. Big M Drug Mart Ltd.,
1985 CanLII 69 (SCC)
, [1985] 1 S.C.R. 295,
[1985] S.C.J. No. 17, at paras.
94 and 95
. One person's
freedom of religion necessarily implies for that person freedom
from someone else's religion. Therefore, the belief, that
certain conduct is required [page751] for religious reasons,
must be freely held. An inquiry in that regard is therefore
appropriate.

[
95
] It is not appropriate to rule on the validity or
veracity of the religious belief or engage in a doctrinal
analysis of the religious practice: see Amselem, supra, at
para.
49
.

[
96
] People's religious beliefs and practices change over
time. Past religious beliefs or practices are only helpful to
the extent that they permit an inference about the applicant's
present religious beliefs or practices: see Amselem, supra, at
para.
53
.

[
97
] The Human Rights Commission, at para. 22 of its factum,
suggested the following types of evidence that might prove
helpful. The applicant could provide evidence concerning the
nature of her belief and answer questions about whether her
beliefs are consistent with current practices. The applicant
could provide evidence from third-party references to verify
current practices. The applicant could provide evidence from
other adherents or religious officials or experts concerning
her beliefs. The Human Rights Commission pointed out and I
agree that the inability to provide this evidence should not be
conclusive. Put another way, this type of evidence is helpful
but not mandatory.

[
98
] At this stage of the inquiry, the fact that the
applicant has a driver's licence with her unveiled photograph
on it can be explored. It appears that this fact was presented
to the preliminary inquiry judge on October 16, 2008. His
Honour appears to have assumed that the applicant's conduct was
inconsistent with her belief. Respectfully, this occurred
because the belief was not explored. It may be that obtaining a
driver's licence is consistent with the applicant's beliefs.
For example, if one of the applicant's children were suddenly
injured in front of the applicant's home, it is highly unlikely
that the applicant would be precluded for religious reasons
from coming to her child's assistance until she put on a veil.
The limits and exceptions to the applicant's religious belief
were never explored and they should be before the court decides
whether obtaining a driver's licence demonstrates that the
applicant is hypocritical or insincere.

[
99
] A dispensation from the strictures of a belief or
practice may be possible. Because the limits and exceptions to
the applicant's belief were not explored, we do not know if a
dispensation is possible to permit the prosecution of two adult
men who, on the applicant's evidence, repeatedly sexually
abused a child from the time she was six years old. If a
religious dispensation is available, then that evidence may
lead to a conclusion that the applicant's reason for insisting
on wearing a veil when she is cross-examined is not religious.
[page752]

[
100
] At this stage of the inquiry, the applicant's statement
that she would be more comfortable not revealing her face to
her uncle can also be explored. On the one hand, women in
Canada testify in sexual assault matters daily without wearing
a veil. The experience is decidedly uncomfortable. Their
discomfort is permitted because our criminal law places a value
on testing evidence. The failure to explore the limits and
exceptions of the applicant's professed religious belief may
have resulted in the preliminary inquiry judge
mischaracterizing the applicant's evidence as an assertion that
wearing the veil was a matter of comfort.

[
101
] At the risk of stating the obvious, if the preliminary
inquiry judge is not satisfied by the applicant that she is
wearing a veil for a religious or other valid reason, he has
the authority pursuant to
s. 537(1)
to order her to remove it,
provided he is satisfied that he must make such an order to
regulate the preliminary inquiry in a way consistent with the

Criminal Code
.
Cross-Examination

[
102
] The second question which the preliminary inquiry judge
must decide arises only if he decides that the applicant is
wearing her veil for a religious or other valid reason. His
Honour must then decide whether he can comply with
s. 540(1)
if
the applicant is veiled when she testifies. Specifically, he
must decide whether the applicant can be cross-examined as that
term is understood in that subsection.

[
103
] His Honour should conduct a second hearing within the
preliminary inquiry to determine this question. The applicant
should be called and examined in chief by the Crown Attorney
and counsel for the defendants should attempt to cross-examine.
The applicant should testify concerning the substance of the
charges. The applicant should testify with her veil on because
to order her at this stage to take it off would prejudge the
matter.

[
104
] The question of what is meant by cross-examination in
the context of s. 540(1) was considered by Mr. Justice
Callaghan (as he then was) in the case of R. v. Durette,
1979 CanLII 2982 (ON HCJ)
, [1979]
O.J. No. 862, 47 C.C.C. (2d) 170 (H.C.J.). In that case, the
main Crown witness testified in chief in the absence of counsel
for one of the defendants. When the defence counsel arrived at
the preliminary inquiry, he was compelled by the provincial
judge to cross-examine the witness even though he had been
absent. The accused was committed for trial and moved to quash.
The application was successful. Mr. Justice Callaghan held that
the right of cross-examination afforded by
s. 540(1)
is the
right to a full, detailed and careful cross-examination based
on a known examination in chief. Justice Callaghan also
observed that it was of particular [page753] importance that
such a right be afforded in relation to the main Crown witness.

[
105
] Section 540(1) does not expand the scope of cross-
examination at a preliminary inquiry. It is only declaratory
of the right to cross-examine: see R. v. Dawson, [1997] O.J.
No. 2188,
1997 CanLII 12348 (Gen. Div.)
, at para.
68
(per Watt
J., as he then was).

[
106
] At the preliminary inquiry in September 2008, counsel
for the defendants relied upon two cases: R. v. Cover,
1988 CanLII 7118 (ON HCJ)
, [1988]
O.J. No. 1615, 44 C.C.C. (3d) 34 (H.C.J.) and R. v. George
(1991),
1991 CanLII 7233 (ON CA)
, 5 O.R. (3d) 144, [1991] O.J. No. 1704, 69 C.C.C.
(3d) 148 (C.A.). R. v. Cover dealt with a situation in which
the preliminary inquiry judge refused to permit cross-
examination of a police officer concerning the information
used as a basis for obtaining a search warrant. The refusal to
permit any cross-examination on that issue was held to be a
deprivation of the right to cross-examine required by s. 540(1)
and resulted in the committal for trial being quashed. R. v.
George dealt with a situation where the preliminary inquiry
judge permitted cross-examination on the basis for a warrant
but in the process disallowed certain questions on that
subject. The Court of Appeal ruled that the disallowance of a
line of questioning did not affect the preliminary inquiry
judge's jurisdiction and confirmed the preliminary inquiry
judge's decision committing the defendant for trial. Neither of
these cases is helpful.

[
107
] At the conclusion of that hearing, His Honour will,
after hearing argument, decide whether cross-examination, as
that term is understood in
s. 540(1)
, has taken place. If he
decides that it has, then the evidence offered by the applicant
will be admitted at the preliminary inquiry subject to any
arguments about relevancy. If His Honour is of the view that
cross-examination has not taken place, the evidence will not be
admitted at the preliminary inquiry. His Honour cannot admit
the applicant's evidence in the absence of cross-examination
because
s. 540(1)
is a mandatory provision and failure to
comply with it will result in a loss of jurisdiction.
Demeanour

[
108
] Argument on the question of cross-examination will
invariably touch upon demeanour. Demeanour has generally been
demeaned as a tool of judicial decision-making: see R. v.
Norman (1993),
1993 CanLII 3387 (ON CA)
, 16 O.R. (3d) 295, [1993] O.J. No. 2802, 87
C.C.C. (3d) 153 (C.A.); The Commission Proceedings Involving G.
Paul Morin -- The Commissioner's Recommendation 76A(b); R. v.
Levert,
2001 CanLII 8606 (ON CA)
, [2001] O.J. No. 3907, 159 C.C.C. (3d) 71 (C.A.), at p.
81 C.C.C. [page754]

[
109
] Lawyers are not judges. Cross-examining is not judging.
It would be more helpful for the court to hear argument on the
question of the utility of visual cues on cross-examination. In
this regard, one should not forget that there are and have been
blind barristers.

[
110
] There were some submissions concerning demeanour when
this matter was first argued on September 10, 2008.
Specifically, counsel for M----D. S. said "seeing the demeanour
of the witness is a matter of critical importance not only at
the trial but also at the preliminary inquiry. My cross-
examination is determined by my assessment of the demeanour
of the witness. I may be pursuing a certain line of questioning
for the witness. Having an opportunity to see their demeanour I
might conclude I believe the witness is being sincere on this
point and am I really going to get anywhere with this line of
questioning. No. I do not think so. I am going to move on to
somewhere else. On the other hand upon observing the witness's
demeanour I might conclude that the witness is prevaricating,
the witness is not being forthright and I might want to explore
that area further."

[
111
] Assuming the reliability of this extraordinary power of
perception, if this is the only aspect of cross-examination
that is interfered with, then the effect of the veil on cross-
examination is minimal.

[
112
] Firstly, the failure to explore the limits of the
witnesses' evidence at a preliminary inquiry simply because one
thinks the witness is telling the truth will almost always be
problematic at trial. To pick an obvious example, where the
witness is "telling the truth", it is important to know what
matters are within the witness's personal knowledge and what
matters are not. It is important to know whether the "truthful"
evidence is based in any way on an assumption or a false
premise. In addition, at the risk of belabouring the obvious,
the truth may be more problematic at a criminal trial than a
lie.

[
113
] Secondly, if what counsel meant by "explore that area
further" was a direct confrontation with an "untruthful"
witness, that tactic was commented upon by Mr. Justice G.
Arthur Martin in R. v. Arviv (1985),
1985 CanLII 161 (ON CA)
, 51 O.R. (2d) 551, [1985]
O.J. No. 2602, 19 C.C.C. (3d) 395 (C.A.) [at para. 30]:

Cross-examination at a preliminary hearing rarely involves a
frontal attack on the credibility of a witness, since the
provincial court judge conducting a preliminary hearing is
not entitled to determine the credibility of witnesses, but
is required to commit for trial if there is any evidence
which, if believed, could result in a conviction.
Consequently, cross-examination of witnesses at a preliminary
hearing is usually and wisely confined to tying the witness
down so that he cannot add additional conversations and
events at the trial, or committing him to facts which can be
contradicted by other evidence. [page755]

[
114
] Mr. Justice Martin did not purport to state that cross-
examination concerning credibility at the preliminary
inquiry was prohibited. He simply said it was rare and probably
unsound.

[
115
] Counsel for the defendant on this application did not
refer to these submissions.

[
116
] A minimal insignificant interference with the right to
cross-examine would no more violate s. 540(1) than would the
improper disallowance of a question.

[
117
] These directions have been confined to verifying the
voluntariness, sincerity and religious nature of the
applicant's belief as well as cross-examination because they
are to be applied at a preliminary inquiry.
Meaningful Judicial Review

[
118
] In order to permit meaningful judicial review, the
testimony of the applicant on this second hearing within the
preliminary inquiry will be videotaped.
Considerations on this Application

[
119
] A judge of the Superior Court granting prerogative
relief has jurisdiction to grant an additional remedy pursuant
to s. 24(1): see R. v. Mills, supra, at para.
267
. I cannot
resort to s. 24(1) to resolve the conflict between the
protected rights of the applicant and the defendant until the
applicant's claim that wearing the veil is an expression of her
religious beliefs and the defendant's assertion that attempting
to cross-examine a veiled witness at a preliminary inquiry
infringes his right to defend himself have been properly
established. I could have directed that the applicant testify
on this application concerning both her belief and the
substance of the charges and permitted the defendant to attempt
to cross-examine and then given directions. I declined that
option because I do not think I should use s. 24(1) to in
effect conduct a portion of the preliminary inquiry. If I did
that, I would have to direct His Honour to substitute my
judgment for his own. His Honour would then complete the
preliminary inquiry and decide whether to commit or discharge.
In effect, the preliminary inquiry would have been conducted by
two judges, which is absurd.

[
120
] If I were to give directions permitting or denying the
veiled testimony without seeing it, the argument concerning
cross-examination is essentially speculation. Speculation is
not helpful. From the applicant's perspective, speculation
decontextualizes the issue. Speaking about the matter in the
abstract not only undervalues but also renders invisible a
professed deeply held religious belief. From the defendants'
perspective, the court [page756] would be deciding that the
applicant can be effectively cross-examined wearing her veil
without the slightest idea of what her testimony about the
substance of the charges sounds and looks like. If this matter
is dealt with in the abstract, there is a great risk that the
resulting judgment will be nothing more than a personal
opinion.

[
121
] The administration of criminal justice functions on
evidence. In this case, the only effective evidence is the
videotaped questioning of the applicant about the substance of
the charges. A principled analysis of this question is only
possible once this evidence is created.
Considerations at Trial

[
122
] Considerations at trial will be at once both the same
and different.

[
123
] The trial judge will have to make the same two
determinations. The decision of the preliminary inquiry judge
will not be relevant in the same way that a decision by a
preliminary inquiry judge concerning the voluntariness of a
statement submitted at the preliminary hearing is not helpful
when the same statement is submitted at trial. This is not the
time and place to comment on that time and resource wasting
principle.

[
124
] Unlike the preliminary inquiry judge, the trial judge
will be a court of competent jurisdiction and therefore able to
balance competing
Charter
values. In addition, the trial judge
will be able to consider this question from perspectives other
than the right to cross-examination. For example, one could
characterize the issue here as disclosure related. The right to
the disclosure of relevant evidence is also protected by
s. 7

of the Charter. The assertion would be that disclosure includes
not only what a dispositive witness will say but also what she
looks like when she says it.

[
125
] There is one decision which may assist trial judges. It
occurred in New Zealand before Judge L H Moore of the New
Zealand District Court at Auckland. Judge Moore was conducting
a criminal trial. He was not conducting a preliminary inquiry.

[
126
] Judge Moore was trying the case of Police v. Razamjoo,
[2005] DCR 408 (N.Z. Dist. Ct.). In that case, the defendant
Abdul Razamjoo reported to the police that his car had been
stolen. He then made a claim on his insurance and was
reimbursed for the stolen car. Police then located Mr.
Razamjoo's car at the address of his friend and countryman Mr.
Salim. Mr. Salim told the police that Mr. Razamjoo had asked
him to sell the car. [page757]

[
127
] The police charged Abdul Razamjoo with falsely
reporting to them that his car had been stolen and with fraud
on his insurance company. At the trial, the prosecutor proposed
to call Mr. Salim's wife as a witness. Mrs. Salim attended to
give evidence wearing a burqa. The defence objected claiming it
could not cross-examine her.

[
128
] Judge Moore heard evidence from both Mr. Salim and his
wife before deciding whether Mrs. Salim would have to remove
her burqa. Mr. Salim testified that he and his wife were
moderately strict Muslims. He testified that he came to New
Zealand as a refugee from Afghanistan and three years later was
joined by his wife. Their beliefs required that, when Mrs.
Salim was in public or in the presence of men other than very
close relatives of her husband or herself, she was required to
wear her burqa. The evidence was that in their home there was a
sitting room for those who could properly view Mrs. Salim when
she was not wearing her burqa and another sitting room for use
by others. These and other arrangements expressed the religious
views of Mr. and Mrs. Salim.

[
129
] Judge Moore also received evidence from Professor
Morris, a professor of religious studies at Victoria University
in New Zealand who offered evidence concerning the Muslim
practice of veiling women. Professor Morris, coincidently, was
partly educated in Canada.

[
130
] Like this case, there was no meaningful compromise
suggested. Like this case, Mrs. Salim was photographed for her
driver's licence with her face uncovered. Like Canada, New
Zealand has a Bill of Rights which guarantees freedom of
conscience and religion.

[
131
] Judge Moore had the benefit of receiving evidence from
Mrs. Salim while she was wearing a burqa. His experience was
that a sense of her character emerged much more slowly than it
did with witnesses who could be seen. He observed that there
was a strong sense of disembodiment, far greater than arises
when receiving evidence by video-link or the playing of a
videotaped statement. He described the experience that he had
as slightly unreal. It was Judge Moore's belief, based on his
experience as a trial judge and on what he saw and heard from
Mrs. Salim, that evidence given from within a burqa would have
less impact than evidence from a person whose face could be
seen.

[
132
] The word "burqa" was not used to describe what the
applicant wore at the preliminary inquiry in this matter. The
word used to describe the veil was "niqab". At the preliminary
inquiry, counsel for M----D. S. said and no objection was taken
to his [page758] statement that "the complainant . . . wears a
veil which covers her face". Judge Moore did not describe the
burqa.

[
133
] Judge Moore ultimately concluded that it would be
contrary to the interests of justice to require that Mrs. Salim
and others like her have their faces exposed to the view of the
public and the defendant while giving evidence. He also
concluded that for him to authorize the giving of evidence from
beneath a covering would be such a major departure from
accepted process and the values of a free and democratic
society that it would seriously risk bringing the District
Court into disrepute. He accepted the fact that there might be
circumstances involving state security or informants that could
justify receiving evidence from a person whose face was hidden,
however he expressed the hope that such instances would be
rare.

[
134
] Judge Moore came to the conclusion that an acceptable
solution in his court was to require Mrs. Salim to give
evidence with her face uncovered. She would do so in such a way
that only the judge, counsel and court staff would be able to
observe her face. The defendant would not be permitted to see
her face.
Conclusion

[
135
] As can be seen from Judge Moore's decision, a trial
judge will have to consider other societal interests in
addition to freedom of religion and the right to cross-examine.
It may be that Canadians would not believe, despite judicial
pronouncements concerning its unreliability, that you can know
fully what a person is saying without seeing the person.

[
136
] There is the practical problem of making sure that
control of the proceedings remains with counsel and the trial
judge and does not shift to the witness.

[
137
] One can also appreciate that the impact of veiled
testimony will vary from witness to witness. In addition to
personal differences, there will also be contextual
differences. In the Razamjoo case, Mrs. Salim was a Crown
witness. Her evidence was corroborative but not essential. In
this case, the applicant's evidence is vital to a successful
prosecution and the charges are not property related, but
historical sexual assaults which, according to the applicant,
began when she was six years old.

[
138
] Canada is not alone in dealing with religious beliefs
which require women be veiled or otherwise distinctively
attired for religious purposes. For example, in Sahin v. Turkey
(2005), 19 BHRC 590, [2006] E.L.R. 73 (Grand Chamber,
E.C.H.R.), the European Court of Human Rights found that the
prohibition on wearing Islamic head scarves at Istanbul
University was not a breach of the applicant's religious
rights. [page759] In R. v. Governors of Denbigh High School,

[2006] UKHL 15, [2007] 1 A.C. 100 (H.L.)
, which concerned
the refusal to permit a student to wear a particular form of
Islamic dress in breach of school uniform rules, the House of
Lords found that there was no breach of the student's religious
rights. In Hudoyberganova v. Uzbekistan (Communication 931/
2000: Hudoyberganova v. Uzbekistan, January 18, 2005,
U.N.H.R. Comm.)), UN Human Rights Committee found the
prohibition on wearing head scarves at Tashkent State Institute
was a breach of religious rights under art. 18 of the
International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. I refer
to these decisions simply to demonstrate that this issue is
international. I do not refer to the decisions because they
have any precedential value.

[
139
] Deeply rooted Canadian cultural values are reflected in
our criminal laws. They manifest themselves in this case where
the Toronto police were sufficiently sensitive to the
complainant's circumstances that they reinvestigated a matter
that they had closed 17 years ago and decided to proceed with
the charges that indirectly cause us to be here.

[
140
] The Canadian approach to sexual assault matters has
resulted in accommodations in the form of closed-circuit
television testimony and testimonial screens. The Canadian
approach has resulted in laws addressing the misuse of false
mythology in cross-examination in sexual assault cases.

[
141
] The Canadian approach for the past 40 years has been to
pursue a multicultural immigration policy. I can take judicial
notice of the fact that the results of that policy have at the
very least created a multicultural society in the Toronto
region where I sit and this application arose. We cannot have a
group within our society which is invisible to the criminal
justice system due to its religious beliefs. At the same time,
we cannot have accommodations which, for a minority of
Canadians, increase the number of identity markers and lead to
a self-selected segregation.

[
142
] The Canadian approach may be a compromise. Perhaps it
will be similar to the one fashioned by Judge Moore in New
Zealand. We cannot proceed to consider that until a preliminary
inquiry has taken place and it has been established by evidence
that the legal
Charter
right not to be deprived of liberty
except in accordance with the principles of fundamental justice
and the Charter guarantee of a fundamental freedom of
conscience and religion are competing with each other: see
Dagenais v. Canadian Broadcasting Corp.,
1994 CanLII 39 (SCC)
, [1994] 3 S.C.R. 835,
[1994] S.C.J. No. 104, at p. 877 S.C.R. [page760]

[
143
] Judge Weisman's decision that the applicant should
testify at the preliminary inquiry without a veil is quashed.
Two hearings to determine the admissibility of the applicant's
veiled testimony will be conducted. The hearing concerning the
substance of the allegations will be videotaped in accordance
with these reasons. The request for an order that the applicant
be permitted to testify at the preliminary inquiry itself
proper while wearing a veil is refused.

Application granted in part.
